posters.title: 4 FÄLLE
posters.subtitle: THE FOUR CASES — WHO DOES WHAT TO WHOM
posters.how_it_works: English shows who does what with word order: the man bites the dog is different from the dog bites the man. German shows it by changing the word THE. The subject is nominative, the direct object accusative, the receiver dative, the owner genitive. Once you read the article, word order becomes flexible.

posters.title: EIN KEIN NICHT
posters.subtitle: A / NOT A / NOT — SAYING NO IN GERMAN
posters.how_it_works: German has two ways to say not. KEIN negates a noun: it means not a or no, and it takes the same endings as EIN. NICHT negates everything else: verbs, adjectives, places, or a specific noun with THE. Rule of thumb: if English says not a or no thing, use kein. Otherwise use nicht.

posters.subtitle: TO BE AND TO HAVE — THE TWO ENGINES OF GERMAN

posters.title: WORTSTELLUNG
posters.subtitle: WORD ORDER — THE VERB IS ALWAYS SECOND
posters.how_it_works: In a German statement the conjugated verb sits in position two — always. Position one can be the subject, the time, or the place; whatever you promote to the front, the verb stays second and the subject slips behind it. Questions put the verb first. And after little words like weil, dass and ob, the verb runs to the very end of the clause.

posters.title: DU / SIE
posters.subtitle: THE TWO YOUS — GERMANY
posters.how_it_works: German splits English you in two. DU is for friends, family, children and animals. SIE (always capital) is for strangers, officials, shops and colleagues until invited otherwise. The verb changes with it: du kommst but Sie kommen. When unsure, use Sie — too formal is polite, too informal is rude. Wait for the older or senior person to offer du.

posters.title: IM RESTAURANT
posters.subtitle: ORDERING, PAYING, TIPPING — START TO FINISH
posters.how_it_works: A German restaurant visit follows a script. You seat yourself or ask for a table, the waiter says Was darf es sein?, you order with Ich nehme or Ich möchte, and at the end you ask for the bill at the table — it will not come by itself. Tipping: round up and say the total you want to pay, or say Stimmt so — keep the change.

posters.title: DER KÖRPER
posters.subtitle: BODY PARTS — AND HOW TO SAY WHERE IT HURTS
posters.how_it_works: Learn body parts with their articles and plurals — many are irregular: der Fuß becomes die Füße, die Hand becomes die Hände. To say something hurts, use tut weh: Mein Kopf tut weh, my head hurts. For plurals use tun weh: Meine Füße tun weh. At the pharmacy or doctor, these two patterns carry the whole conversation.

Days and parts of the day take am: am Montag, am Morgen. Clock times take um: um drei Uhr. Months and seasons take im: im Januar, im Sommer.

posters.title: ZAHLEN
posters.subtitle: NUMBERS — GERMANS SAY THEM BACKWARDS
posters.how_it_works: From 21 to 99, German swaps the digits: 21 is einundzwanzig — one-and-twenty. Say the ones digit first, then und, then the tens. Watch three irregulars: sechzehn drops the s of sechs, siebzehn shortens sieben, and dreißig ends in -ssig sound spelt ß. Everything else is regular stacking.

posters.title: KLEIDUNG
posters.subtitle: CLOTHING — AND TWO FAMOUS SINGULAR TRAPS

Dressing uses separable verbs you already know: anziehen (put on), ausziehen (take off): Ich ziehe die Jacke an. To say what you wear, use tragen: Ich trage eine Brille.

posters.title: DER AKKUSATIV
posters.subtitle: WHY DER SOMETIMES BECOMES DEN
posters.how_it_works: When a noun is the DIRECT OBJECT — the thing being seen, bought, eaten — German changes its article. The good news: only the masculine changes. der becomes den, ein becomes einen. Feminine, neuter and plural stay exactly the same. This is why you order einen Kaffee: the coffee is the thing you are getting.

posters.title: MODALVERBEN
posters.subtitle: CAN, MUST, WANT — THE SIX POWER VERBS
posters.how_it_works: Six verbs unlock hundreds of sentences: können (can), müssen (must), wollen (want), dürfen (may), sollen (should), möchten (would like). The modal takes position 2 and the main verb flies TO THE END in its dictionary form: Ich kann heute nicht kommen. Learn the ich/du/er row of each — ich and er are always identical.

posters.title: TRENNBARE VERBEN
posters.subtitle: THE PREFIX CATAPULT — VERBS THAT SPLIT IN TWO
posters.how_it_works: Many German verbs carry a prefix that BREAKS OFF and flies to the end of the sentence: aufstehen (to get up) becomes Ich stehe um sieben auf. The stressed prefix always separates in the present tense. With a modal verb the pair stays glued together at the end: Ich muss morgen früh aufstehen. In the Perfekt, ge- slips INSIDE: aufgestanden, eingekauft.

posters.title: ICH DU SIE

posters.title: WORTSTELLUNG
posters.subtitle: ONE LAW: THE VERB IS ALWAYS SECOND
posters.how_it_works: German main clauses obey one iron law: the conjugated verb sits in POSITION 2. Anything can take position 1 — the subject, the time, the place — and everything else shuffles, but the verb does not move. Yes-no questions flip the verb to position 1. And weil (because) breaks the law on purpose: it kicks the verb to the very end.

posters.title: DER DATIV
posters.subtitle: THE THIRD CASE — DEM, DER, DEM
posters.how_it_works: The dative marks the receiver or the setting: to whom, with what, where. posters.title: EIN ROTER ROCK
posters.subtitle: ADJECTIVE ENDINGS — THE SURVIVABLE STARTER KIT
posters.how_it_works: An adjective BEFORE a noun needs an ending. Here is the whole A1 story in two rules. After der, die, das just add -e: der rote Rock. After ein, the adjective itself must show the gender, because ein does not: ein roter Rock, eine rote Jacke, ein rotes Kleid. After the sentence, adjectives stay naked: Der Rock ist rot.

posters.title: UND ABER WEIL
posters.subtitle: GLUE WORDS — AND WHAT THEY DO TO THE VERB
posters.how_it_works: Connectors come in two tribes. The friendly four — und, aber, oder, denn — sit at position zero and change NOTHING about word order. The verb-kickers — weil, dass, wenn — send the verb to the very end of their clause. Same meaning, different mechanics: denn and weil both mean because, but watch where the verb lands.

posters.title: GEFÜHLE
posters.subtitle: FEELINGS — AND THE MIR IST TRAP
posters.how_it_works: Most feelings work like English: Ich bin müde, I am tired. But temperature and wellbeing use MIR — to me: Mir ist kalt means I am cold. Say Ich bin kalt and you have just told everyone you are a cold-hearted person. The same pattern gives you Mir ist schlecht, I feel sick — one of the most useful sentences in the language.

posters.title: DIE FAMILIE
posters.subtitle: THE FAMILY — WHO IS WHO
posters.how_it_works: Family words come in gendered pairs: der Bruder, die Schwester. Two collective words have no English twin: die Geschwister means brothers-and-sisters together, die Eltern means parents. Watch der Mann and die Frau — they mean man and woman, but ALSO husband and wife: meine Frau is my wife.

posters.title: EINKAUFEN
posters.subtitle: SHOPPING — SHOPS, AMOUNTS AND THE COUNTER SCRIPT
posters.how_it_works: German shopping runs on specialist shops and precise amounts. You buy bread at the Bäckerei, medicine at the Apotheke, and you order cheese by the hundred grams. The counter script never changes: the assistant asks what you want, you answer with Ich hätte gern..., they ask Sonst noch etwas? — anything else — and you close with Das ist alles.

posters.title: BERUF + ARBEIT
posters.subtitle: JOBS AND WORK — SAY YOUR JOB WITHOUT AN ARTICLE
posters.how_it_works: The number one trap: German states professions WITHOUT an article. Ich bin Lehrer — I am teacher, not a teacher. Most jobs add -in for women: der Lehrer, die Lehrerin. And learn der Feierabend — the moment work ends and the evening begins. There is no English word for it, but there is a whole feeling.

posters.title: DER WEG
posters.subtitle: DIRECTIONS — LEFT, RIGHT, STRAIGHT ON
posters.how_it_works: Three words carry every route: links (left), rechts (right), geradeaus (straight on). Ask with Wie komme ich zum...? for masculine and neuter places or zur... for feminine ones. Answers come as commands in the Sie-form: Gehen Sie geradeaus, nehmen Sie die zweite Straße links. Landmarks do the rest: the traffic light, the crossing, the church.

posters.title: BEIM ARZT
posters.subtitle: DOCTOR AND PHARMACY — SAY WHERE IT HURTS
posters.how_it_works: Two patterns handle almost everything: Ich habe + noun for symptoms — Ich habe Fieber, Ich habe Kopfschmerzen — and any body part + tut weh for pain. Add -schmerzen to a body part and you have named the ache: Halsschmerzen, Bauchschmerzen. At the pharmacy, ask Haben Sie etwas gegen...? — do you have something against...?

Activities you go and do take gehen plus the infinitive: Ich gehe schwimmen. To say you LIKE doing something, drop gern after the verb: Ich koche gern. Prefer something? lieber. Love it most? am liebsten.

German life also runs on appointments and forms: the Amt is any government office, the Termin is sacred, and the Formular always wants one more Unterschrift — signature.

Outdoors, one pair will trip you: der See is the LAKE, die See is the SEA — same word, the article changes the water. And learn wandern early: hiking is not a hobby in Germany, it is a national institution.

posters.how_it_works: Good wishes in German are fixed formulas — you cannot build them word by word, you must know them. The all-purpose ones: Alles Gute (all the best), Viel Glück (good luck), Viel Spaß (have fun). At New Year Germans wish each other a good SLIDE into the new year: Guten Rutsch! And note: German Christmas happens on the EVENING of the 24th — Heiligabend.

posters.title: ORDINALZAHLEN

posters.subtitle: THE MAN WHO — DER DIE DAS AS THAT / WHICH / WHO
posters.how_it_works: A relative clause describes a noun. The relative pronoun matches gender and number of that noun, and takes the case of its job inside the clause. Der Mann, der dort steht. Die Frau, die ich kenne. Das Haus, in dem ich wohne. The verb goes to the end of the clause. Use wo for places, was after alles/nichts/das.

posters.title: ZU + INFINITIV
posters.subtitle: I TRY TO — THE LITTLE ZU BEFORE THE VERB
posters.how_it_works: After many verbs and adjectives German uses zu + infinitive: Ich versuche zu kommen. Separable verbs put zu in the middle: aufzustehen. um…zu means in order to. ohne…zu means without doing. Instead of to is statt…zu. No zu after modal verbs or after gehen/lernen in Ich gehe schwimmen.

Perfect passive is sein + worden: Das Brot ist gebacken worden. German uses the passive for processes, notices, and when the doer does not matter. A2 needs recognition and a few set phrases more than free production.

cards.section: a pictogram sentence diagram, full width
cards.rule: English shows who does what with word order: the man bites the dog is different from the dog bites the man. German shows it by changing the word THE. The subject is nominative, the direct object accusative, the receiver dative, the owner genitive. Once you read the article, word order becomes flexible.

German has two ways to say not. KEIN negates a noun: it means not a or no, and it takes the same endings as EIN. NICHT negates everything else: verbs, adjectives, places, or a specific noun with THE. Rule of thumb: if English says not a or no thing, use kein. Otherwise use nicht.

You will use them in almost every sentence and later to build the past tense. Do not translate form by form — memorise each line as a complete sound.

cards.english: I am going to Berlin tomorrow.
cards.rule: In a German statement the conjugated verb sits in position two — always. Position one can be the subject, the time, or the place; whatever you promote to the front, the verb stays second and the subject slips behind it. Questions put the verb first. And after little words like weil, dass and ob, the verb runs to the very end of the clause.

German splits English you in two. DU is for friends, family, children and animals. SIE (always capital) is for strangers, officials, shops and colleagues until invited otherwise. The verb changes with it: du kommst but Sie kommen. When unsure, use Sie — too formal is polite, too informal is rude. Wait for the older or senior person to offer du.

Many German verbs carry a prefix that snaps off: anrufen means to phone, but in a sentence the AN flies to the end: Ich rufe dich an — I phone you. Think of English phrasal verbs said backwards: I call you UP. The prefix returns to the front in the infinitive and after weil, dass and ob.

cards.section: the nine prepositions as a strip; each cell holds a tiny black pictogram of a dot positioned relative to a square (dot beside, on top, behind, inside, next to, above, under, in front, between) with the word and gloss
cards.rule: Nine prepositions can take two cases. If you are STAYING somewhere, use the dative — answering WO, where. If you are MOVING somewhere, use the accusative — answering WOHIN, where to. English does the same with in and into. One question decides the case every single time: is anything changing location?

A German restaurant visit follows a script. You seat yourself or ask for a table, the waiter says Was darf es sein?, you order with Ich nehme or Ich möchte, and at the end you ask for the bill at the table — it will not come by itself. Tipping: round up and say the total you want to pay, or say Stimmt so — keep the change.

Learn body parts with their articles and plurals — many are irregular: der Fuß becomes die Füße, die Hand becomes die Hände. To say something hurts, use tut weh: Mein Kopf tut weh, my head hurts. For plurals use tun weh: Meine Füße tun weh. At the pharmacy or doctor, these two patterns carry the whole conversation.

The big trap: halb vier is HALF TO four, meaning 3:30 — not half past four. Germans count toward the coming hour. Viertel nach is quarter past, Viertel vor is quarter to. Days and parts of the day take am: am Montag, am Morgen. Clock times take um: um drei Uhr. Months and seasons take im: im Januar, im Sommer.

From 21 to 99, German swaps the digits: 21 is einundzwanzig — one-and-twenty. Say the ones digit first, then und, then the tens. Watch three irregulars: sechzehn drops the s of sechs, siebzehn shortens sieben, and dreißig ends in -ssig sound spelt ß. Everything else is regular stacking.

When a noun is the DIRECT OBJECT — the thing being seen, bought, eaten — German changes its article. The good news: only the masculine changes. der becomes den, ein becomes einen. Feminine, neuter and plural stay exactly the same. This is why you order einen Kaffee: the coffee is the thing you are getting.

cards.english: Ich stehe um sieben auf. — I get up at seven.
cards.rule: Many German verbs carry a prefix that BREAKS OFF and flies to the end of the sentence: aufstehen (to get up) becomes Ich stehe um sieben auf. The stressed prefix always separates in the present tense. With a modal verb the pair stays glued together at the end: Ich muss morgen früh aufstehen. In the Perfekt, ge- slips INSIDE: aufgestanden, eingekauft.

cards.english: Ich habe das gemacht. — I did that.
cards.rule: Spoken German uses the Perfekt for the past: a helper verb in position 2 plus a ge- participle at the very end. Most verbs take haben. Verbs of MOVEMENT or CHANGE take sein: gone, driven, flown, got up. One famous exception: bleiben (to stay) takes sein although nobody moves anywhere.

German has two words for YOU. Use du with family, friends, children, students and animals. Use Sie — always capitalised, always with the plural verb form — with strangers, officials, shop staff and colleagues until they offer you du. When in doubt, start with Sie: too polite is a much smaller mistake than too familiar.

German main clauses obey one iron law: the conjugated verb sits in POSITION 2. Anything can take position 1 — the subject, the time, the place — and everything else shuffles, but the verb does not move. Yes-no questions flip the verb to position 1. And weil (because) breaks the law on purpose: it kicks the verb to the very end.

Three command forms, one per audience. For du: take the du-form and drop the -st ending — du kommst becomes Komm! For ihr: just use the ihr-form — Kommt! For Sie: verb first, then Sie — Kommen Sie! Bare commands sound harsh; Germans soften them with the little words mal, bitte and doch.

Every adjective climbs a three-step ladder: schnell, schneller, am schnellsten. Add -er for the comparative and am ...-sten for the superlative — German never says mehr schnell the way English says more quickly. Short words with a, o or u usually take an umlaut: alt, älter. A handful are irregular and simply must be learned — gut, besser, am besten leads the list.

Connectors come in two tribes. The friendly four — und, aber, oder, denn — sit at position zero and change NOTHING about word order. The verb-kickers — weil, dass, wenn — send the verb to the very end of their clause. Same meaning, different mechanics: denn and weil both mean because, but watch where the verb lands.

Say Ich bin kalt and you have just told everyone you are a cold-hearted person. The same pattern gives you Mir ist schlecht, I feel sick — one of the most useful sentences in the language.

German greetings run on a clock and a map: Guten Morgen before about 10, Guten Tag until evening, Guten Abend after. In the north you will hear Moin, in the south Servus and Grüß Gott. And one word does five jobs: bitte means please, you are welcome, here you are, pardon?, and go ahead. You cannot overuse it.

German shopping runs on specialist shops and precise amounts. You buy bread at the Bäckerei, medicine at the Apotheke, and you order cheese by the hundred grams. The counter script never changes: the assistant asks what you want, you answer with Ich hätte gern..., they ask Sonst noch etwas? — anything else — and you close with Das ist alles.

The number one trap: German states professions WITHOUT an article. Ich bin Lehrer — I am teacher, not a teacher. Most jobs add -in for women: der Lehrer, die Lehrerin. And learn der Feierabend — the moment work ends and the evening begins. There is no English word for it, but there is a whole feeling.

Three words carry every route: links (left), rechts (right), geradeaus (straight on). Ask with Wie komme ich zum...? for masculine and neuter places or zur... for feminine ones. Answers come as commands in the Sie-form: Gehen Sie geradeaus, nehmen Sie die zweite Straße links. Landmarks do the rest: the traffic light, the crossing, the church.

Two verbs organise most hobbies. Games and instruments take spielen: Ich spiele Fußball, Ich spiele Gitarre — no article needed. Activities you go and do take gehen plus the infinitive: Ich gehe schwimmen. To say you LIKE doing something, drop gern after the verb: Ich koche gern. Prefer something? lieber. Love it most? am liebsten.

German life also runs on appointments and forms: the Amt is any government office, the Termin is sacred, and the Formular always wants one more Unterschrift — signature.

cards.rule: Germany loves cash: many bakeries, kiosks and restaurants still take Bargeld only, so always ask Kann ich mit Karte zahlen? before you order. German life also runs on appointments and forms: the Amt is any government office, the Termin is sacred, and the Formular always wants one more Unterschrift — signature.

Good wishes in German are fixed formulas — you cannot build them word by word, you must know them. The all-purpose ones: Alles Gute (all the best), Viel Glück (good luck), Viel Spaß (have fun). At New Year Germans wish each other a good SLIDE into the new year: Guten Rutsch! And note: German Christmas happens on the EVENING of the 24th — Heiligabend.

A relative clause describes a noun. The relative pronoun matches gender and number of that noun, and takes the case of its job inside the clause. Der Mann, der dort steht. Die Frau, die ich kenne. Das Haus, in dem ich wohne. The verb goes to the end of the clause. Use wo for places, was after alles/nichts/das.

After many verbs and adjectives German uses zu + infinitive: Ich versuche zu kommen. Separable verbs put zu in the middle: aufzustehen. um…zu means in order to. ohne…zu means without doing. Instead of to is statt…zu. No zu after modal verbs or after gehen/lernen in Ich gehe schwimmen.

The present passive is werden + past participle: Das Brot wird gebacken. The agent is von + dative when you need it. Perfect passive is sein + worden: Das Brot ist gebacken worden. German uses the passive for processes, notices, and when the doer does not matter. A2 needs recognition and a few set phrases more than free production.
